title: Leading Paid Staff
subtitle: When you sign a person's paycheck and shepherd their soul at the same time, grace and accountability are bound to meet, and sometimes to collide.

sections.title: You Are Their Pastor and Their Boss
sections.body:
There is no relationship in ministry stranger than the one with paid staff. You are their pastor, charged with their soul. You are also their employer, signing the check that feeds their children. Those two roles pull in different directions, and the pastor who pretends they do not is setting up a wound.

The family business runs into this and so does the church, but the church has it worse, because we wrap the whole thing in the language of family and calling and ministry, which makes the hard parts feel like betrayal when they come. You cannot fire a brother. But sometimes you must release an employee. And he is both, and so are you, and there is no clean way to hold it.

I have gotten this wrong in both directions. I have been so much the pastor that I tolerated work that hurt the church for years, calling my cowardice grace. And I have been so much the boss that I forgot the man in front of me had a soul and a family and a fear of failing. The work is not to collapse the tension. It is to hold both, honestly, and to tell the truth about which one you are doing at any given moment.

sections.title: Hiring Slowly, for the Right Reasons
sections.body:
Most staff problems are hiring problems wearing a later costume. We hire fast because the need is urgent, we hire for gifting and ignore character, we hire the person we like rather than the person who fits, and then we spend years managing a mistake we made in a month.

Hire slowly. Test the person in unpaid work first if you can, because volunteering reveals what an interview hides. Check whether they are humble enough to be led, because a staff member who cannot submit will cost you more than the work is worth, no matter how gifted. Be honest in the hiring about the hard parts of the job, the salary, the expectations, the realities, because a person hired on a half-truth will feel deceived the first time the truth shows up.

And hire for the church, not for your own comfort. The friend who needs a job, the loyal member who wants to go vocational, the family member, these are the hires that feel like grace and end in grief, because you have brought someone in for a reason that has nothing to do with whether they should be there. Grace is real, but a job is not a charity, and a wrong hire made out of kindness becomes an unkindness to the whole staff who must work around them.

sections.title: Leading the People Whose Salary You Sign
sections.body:
Good staff leadership is mostly clarity and follow-through, two things ministry culture is strangely bad at. We are warm and vague, and warmth without clarity is cruelty on a delay, because the person never knows where they stand until the day you finally tell them, and by then it is a crisis.

So be clear. Define the role in writing. Tell people what success looks like and what failure looks like. Give real feedback regularly, the affirming kind and the correcting kind, in normal weeks, so that no correction ever comes as a sudden ambush. The staff member who hears the truth in small doses, often, can grow. The one who hears nothing for two years and then everything at once is being managed by a coward, and I have been that coward.

And lead their souls, genuinely, because you are their pastor. Ask about their marriage, their walk, their burnout. Protect their day off harder than they will. Do not let the church consume the people who serve it, because a staff worked into the ground is a testimony against the gospel you are paying them to proclaim. The accountability and the care are not opposites. The clearest leaders are often the most caring, because clarity is itself a form of love, and vagueness is a form of neglect.

sections.title: When You Have to Let Someone Go
sections.body:
Sometimes you must release a staff member, and it is one of the heaviest things a pastor ever does, because you are removing a person's income and disrupting their sense of calling, and you are doing it to someone you have prayed with.

Do not avoid it. The avoided firing punishes everyone, the church that suffers the poor work, the team that resents carrying it, and the staff member himself, who is kept in a role he is failing at, denied the clarity that might let him find the place he would actually flourish. Cowardice dressed as grace is the most expensive thing in church leadership, and I have paid for it more than once, in morale and in trust and in the slow rot of a team that knows the leader will not act.

When you must do it, do it with both truth and dignity. Be honest about why, do not hide behind vague language that leaves the person confused and suspicious. Be generous in the leaving, severance if you can manage it, a reference where one is honest, time and help to land somewhere new. Protect their reputation, tell the congregation only what is theirs to know and not a word of gossip more. You are still their pastor even as you cease to be their boss, and how you fire a person preaches a sermon about your character louder than anything you say from the pulpit.

sections.title: The Collision You Cannot Always Avoid
sections.body:
There will come a day when grace and accountability genuinely collide, when what is best for the church and what is kindest to the person are not the same thing, and you have to choose. That day is the test of whether you are a leader or only a nice man.

The nice man chooses the person and lets the church suffer, and calls it love. The harsh man chooses the church and discards the person, and calls it leadership. Neither is right. The faithful man chooses what the church needs, because the church is his trust and the staff member is one person among many he is charged to protect, and then he does the hard thing with as much tenderness as the hard thing allows. He tells the truth and weeps while he tells it.

That is the calling. To hold the budget and the soul at once. To be the boss who never stops being the pastor, even in the firing, even in the conflict, even when the two roles tear at each other and there is no clean way through.

It does not resolve. You sign the check and you shepherd the man, and some days those are the same act, and some days they are at war, and you have to choose, and you will lose sleep over the choice. Good. The day you stop losing sleep is the day you have stopped loving one of them.
